fields.Participants: Chief Accountant, AP Supervisor, AR Supervisor, Treasury Analyst, Tax Accountant, Cost Accountant, CFO
fields.Trigger: Last calendar day of the month

steps.activity: Verify all store day-end closings are posted; follow up on any outstanding
AP: Ensure all vendor invoices received before cut-off are entered and matched

GRNI reconciliation: system generates Goods Received Not Invoiced report showing all GRs without matching AP invoices; Finance verifies completeness; if system uses GR/IR clearing account, verify clearing account balance reconciles to open GRNI list; accrue provision for estimated costs where invoices are expected but not yet received
AR: Post all AR invoices and payments received through month-end
Accruals: Book accrual entries for expenses incurred but not yet invoiced (utilities, freight, rent)
Intercompany: Verify all IC transactions are posted; run IC matching

FX Revaluation: System revalues all open foreign-currency AP and AR balances at month-end BIR exchange rate; posts unrealized FX gain/loss to P&L and FX revaluation reserve to BS; auto-reverses the revaluation entries at start of next period
Inventory: Verify perpetual WAC (weighted average cost) calculations; post adjustments from cycle counts

WAC methodology: system calculates perpetual moving average cost at each goods receipt — new WAC = (prior inventory value + receipt value) ÷ (prior quantity + receipt quantity); COGS at POS uses current WAC at time of sale; at month-end, Cost Accountant verifies WAC accuracy by sampling high-value and high-volume SKUs, reconciles total inventory valuation to GL inventory accounts, and posts any adjustments from cycle counts (W6) or physical inventory (W42)
Fixed Assets: Post monthly depreciation
Prepayments: Amortize prepaid expenses (insurance, rent)
Bank reconciliation: Match bank statements to GL cash accounts (all bank accounts, all entities)
Run trial balance per entity; review for unusual balances
Post adjusting entries as needed
Generate preliminary financial statements per entity (BS, IS, CF)
Run intercompany elimination entries for consolidation
Generate consolidated financial statements (5 entities)
CFO reviews consolidated statements; queries variances
Tax Accountant prepares VAT return (BIR 2550M) and withholding tax returns (1601-EQ, 1601-C)

EWT remittance (quarter-end months): Tax Accountant generates EWT remittance file (BIR 1601-EQ) from accumulated Withholding Tax Payable per vendor per ATC; reconciles to vendor remittance list; transmits to BIR via eFPS; system posts remittance (Dr. Withholding Tax Payable / Cr. Cash)

Inventory net realizable value (NRV) review: Cost Accountant runs inventory aging report (days since last sale); for slow-moving items (> 180 days), system compares WAC to estimated NRV (clearance price × sell-through probability); Cost Accountant proposes write-down per SKU where NRV < cost; Controller approves write-downs > PHP 50,000; system posts Dr. Inventory Write-Down Expense / Cr. Inventory Provision (contra-asset); **NRV reversal treatment**: when a written-down item is subsequently sold — (a) system recognizes revenue at selling price (standard), (b) system recognizes COGS at the written-down carrying amount (not the original WAC), (c) difference between original WAC and written-down carrying amount represents the write-down previously recognized; for partial sales of written-down lots, COGS per unit is the written-down unit cost; no additional journal entry is required at point of sale because the provision was already posted; at next quarterly NRV review (W9A.16b), Cost Accountant reassesses remaining written-down items — if NRV has recovered above carrying amount (e.g., market price increase), Cost Accountant may reverse the provision up to the original write-down amount per PAS 2.31 with Controller approval; system posts reversal as Dr. Inventory Provision / Cr. Inventory Write-Down Recovery (P&L); reversal is limited to the original write-down amount per SKU — carrying value cannot exceed original WAC

Local Business Tax (LBT) per LGU: system generates LBT payment schedule per location (200 stores + 4 DCs + HQ) based on configured LGU calendars (annual or quarterly per LGU); Tax Accountant reviews schedule, validates amounts per LGU rate schedules (typically 1–2% of gross receipts for retail, varies by LGU); processes payments per LGU (online, over-the-counter, or LGU office); system posts payment per location (Dr. Local Business Tax Expense / Cr. Cash); tracks payment status and receipt per location; flags locations with upcoming or overdue LBT payments on monthly dashboard

Inventory write-off (obsolete / damaged beyond recovery): distinct from NRV write-down (step 16b) — for items that will never be sold (fully obsolete, expired, irrevocably damaged, or vendor refuses RTV and item has no residual value); Cost Accountant prepares write-off list per SKU with supporting evidence (photos, aging, disposition attempts); tiered approval: Store Manager ≤ PHP 10,000, Controller ≤ PHP 50,000, CFO ≤ PHP 500,000, CEO > PHP 500,000; system posts Dr. Inventory Write-Off Expense (loss) / Cr. Inventory — removes items from inventory register entirely (not a provision — permanent removal); BIR documentation retained: write-off approval, supporting evidence, and physical destruction or disposal certificate

Credit note / debit note reconciliation: Chief Accountant runs AP and AR credit note aging report — all unapplied credit memos and debit memos listed by entity, vendor/customer, age, and amount; credit memos > 60 days unapplied flagged for investigation; AP Clerk contacts vendor to resolve open AP credits (apply to next invoice, request refund, or confirm as settled); AR Clerk contacts customers to resolve open AR credits (apply to next sale, issue refund, or confirm as settled); unresolved items > 90 days escalated to Controller; summary of unapplied credit notes included in month-end close package
steps.r: Chief Accountant / AP Clerk / AR Clerk

steps.activity: Final close: lock period in system

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-validate of "Verify all store day-end closings are posted" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-capture of "entered and matched" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-count of "count, verify clearing account balance reconciles to open GRNI list" (replaces manual Step 2a).
Controls: - CTL-292 (ensure controlled execution — FP&A & Reporting (PA-17.4).)
- operational: Chief Accountant / Controller review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Store day-end posting delays blocking close start**: if any of 200 stores fail to post day-end closings before month-end cut-off, the Chief Accountant cannot begin close activities; store-level posting compliance varies, with provincial stores frequently submitting late

- **GRNI valuation uncertainty during close**: estimating accruals for goods received but not yet invoiced requires judgment; over-accrual understates COGS while under-accrual understates liabilities — both create audit findings

- **Intercompany mismatch blocking consolidation**: unresolved IC discrepancies across 5 entity pairs prevent consolidated statement generation; even small timing differences (PHP 100) block automated elimination entries until manually resolved

- **NRV write-down subjectivity**: determining NRV for slow-moving inventory involves estimating clearance prices and sell-through probabilities; Cost Accountant and Controller may disagree on write-down amounts, especially for seasonal merchandise with uncertain residual value

- **Tax filing deadline compression**: BIR VAT return (2550M) is due by the 20th of the following month, while the close target is 5 working days — this leaves only ~10 days for tax extraction, return preparation, review, and eFPS filing
Pain Points / Risks (Year-End Close — W9: - **External audit timeline compression**: BIR and SEC filing deadlines are fixed; if external auditors (W95) identify issues during Q1 fieldwork, the Finance team must resolve queries while also processing Q1 monthly close, creating severe capacity strain on the ~8–10 people already committed to close activities

- **Wall-to-wall physical inventory disruption**: year-end physical count (step 19) requires all 200 stores + 4 DCs to pause or slow operations for 1–2 days; scheduling a chain-wide count during the holiday retail peak in December is impractical, forcing a January count that creates audit window adjustments

- **13th month pay and statutory bonus reconciliation**: PD 851 mandates 13th month pay for all employees; reconciling accruals against actual payments across ~6,762 employees in 5 entities is error-prone, especially for employees who joined or separated mid-year (W43)

- **Multi-entity consolidation complexity**: year-end elimination entries across 5 entities with goods-based IC transfers (W14), IC loans, and IC dividends require careful matching; any unresolved IC mismatch blocks consolidated statement finalization
Staffing Implication: - **Controller**: Owns the close process. 1 person sufficient with support.
- **1 Chief Accountant**: Handles most close entries. Stretched during close week (~30 hours of close work in 5 days).
- **1 Cost Accountant**: Inventory valuation + fixed assets.
- **1 Tax Accountant**: VAT + withholding monthly; income tax quarterly/annual.
- **Total Finance team (46 per profile §3.3)**: During close week, 8–10 people are heavily involved. The rest of the month is lighter. Current headcount supports this.
System Touchpoints: - Store day-end posting monitoring (W9A.1)
- GRNI reconciliation report and clearing account balance verification (W9A.2a)
- Accrual and journal entry workflow (W9A.4–8, 11)
- IC matching and elimination automation (W9A.5, 13)
- Inventory valuation engine: perpetual WAC verification (not periodic recalculation); month-end reconciliation of inventory valuation to GL (W9A.6a)
- Bank reconciliation (W9A.9)

- Local Business Tax (LBT) per LGU: per-location LBT calendar, payment tracking and schedule; LGU-specific rate schedules and forms; payment status dashboard with overdue alerting; BIR retention of LBT receipts (W9A.16c)
- Multi-entity financial statement generation (W9A.12–14)
- Period lock / close controls (W9A.17)
- BIR tax form generation (W9A.16)
- EWT remittance file generation per BIR 1601-EQ (quarterly) with per-vendor per-ATC breakdown; eFPS transmission (W9A.16a)

- Inventory NRV review: aging by days-since-last-sale, NRV calculator, write-down journal entry with approval, provision reversal on subsequent sale (PAS 2.31 compliant — reversal limited to original write-down; carrying value capped at original WAC; quarterly reassessment with Cost Accountant and Controller review) (W9A.16b)

- Inventory write-off: complete removal from inventory register (not provision); tiered approval with BIR-compliant documentation (photos, aging, disposition evidence, destruction certificate); distinct from NRV write-down (W9A.16d)

- Credit note / debit note reconciliation: AP and AR credit note aging report with unapplied memos > 60 days flagged; escalation at 90 days; resolution tracking (apply, refund, settle); summary in month-end close package (W9A.16e)
Time Estimate: - Store day-end verification and follow-up: ~2 hours (day 1)
- AP invoice cut-off and GRNI reconciliation: ~3 hours (day 1)
- AR invoice posting: ~1 hour (day 1)
- Accruals and prepayments: ~3.5 hours (day 2)
- IC matching and FX revaluation: ~2.5 hours (day 2)
- Inventory WAC verification and adjustments: ~2 hours (day 2–3)
- Bank reconciliation (all entities): ~3 hours (day 3)
- Trial balance, adjusting entries, financial statements: ~2.5 hours (day 3–4)
- Consolidation and elimination entries: ~1.5 hours (day 4)
- CFO review and consolidation sign-off: ~1 hour (day 4–5)
- Tax return preparation (VAT, EWT, CWT): ~5 hours (day 4–5)
- Period lock: ~15 min (day 5)
- NRV review, write-offs, credit note reconciliation: ~4 hours (day 4–5)
- Total close effort: ~30–35 hours over 5 working days across 8–10 people

fields.Trigger: Need identified for asset acquisition (equipment, vehicles, fixtures, IT hardware, store build-out)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-submit of "submits capex request" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-review of "reviews and approves or returns for revision" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-validate of "checks ROI calculation" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-02 (prevent unauthorized capital expenditure.)
- operational: Requesting Department Head review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Quotation gaming for approval threshold avoidance**: requestors may split a PHP 600,000 purchase into two PHP 300,000 requests to stay below the CEO approval threshold (PHP 500,001); without system-level detection of split purchases from the same vendor within a time window, approval tier circumvention goes undetected

- **Capitalization delay for new store build-outs**: during rapid expansion (10–15 new stores/year), hundreds of contractor invoices accumulate against AUC accounts (W276); if the Engineering/Project Manager delays operational handover confirmation (W227), assets remain in AUC without depreciation, understating operating expenses

- **Post-implementation review neglect**: quarterly capex vs. budget reviews (step 9) are often deprioritized in favor of urgent operational issues; without consistent post-implementation discipline, cost overruns on completed projects go undetected and inform future budget estimates inaccurately

- **Fixed asset classification errors**: distinguishing between capitalize (asset) and expense (repair/maintenance) requires judgment; Store Managers may request capex for items that should be expensed (e.g., replacement parts vs. new equipment), inflating the asset base and distorting depreciation schedules
Staffing Implication: - **1 Capex Analyst** (within Finance): 50–80 requests/year. Each requires ~30 min validation. ~40 hours/year = ~1 day/month. Absorbed by existing Finance team (46 per profile §3.3). May be the Cost Accountant or a dedicated analyst role during peak store-opening periods.

- Budget availability check against annual capex budget (W21.3)
- PO creation from approved capex (W21.5)
- Fixed Asset creation and capitalization (W21.7)
- Depreciation schedule auto-generation (W21.8)
- Capex vs. budget reporting (W21.9)

- Approval routing per tier: ~15–30 min/request

workflows.name: Annual Budget Preparation & Monthly Variance Review

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-count of "headcount plan, new store openings" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-generate of "prepare department-level budget" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-review of "review consolidated draft" (replaces manual Step 7).
Controls: - CTL-35 (ensure budget adherence.)
- operational: Controller review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Top-down vs. bottom-up budget misalignment**: CFO/CEO revenue growth expectations may not align with Department Heads' operational reality; negotiations during step 7 are contentious, especially for Store Ops (labor costs) and Merchandising (margin targets), leading to budgets that are either unrealistic or built on forced assumptions

- **Budget rigidity during rapid expansion**: opening 10–15 new stores/year (W16) requires frequent budget revisions (step 13); the quarterly revision cadence may not be fast enough to accommodate mid-quarter new store decisions, leading to capex and opex spending without approved budget coverage

- **Cost center proliferation**: with 200 stores, 4 DCs, HQ departments, and 5 entities, the budget structure has 200+ cost centers and 500–800 GL accounts per entity; maintaining consistent chart of accounts and cost center definitions across entities requires constant governance that is often deprioritized

- **Variance analysis superficiality**: Department Heads may provide generic variance explanations ("due to volume increase") rather than root cause analysis; without CFO challenge during monthly reviews, corrective actions are not identified and budget accuracy does not improve year over year
Staffing Implication: - **Controller**: Owns the budget process. ~30 hours during annual cycle + ~4 hours/month for variance review.
- **Department Heads**: ~3–5 hours each during annual cycle + ~1 hour/month variance review. Absorbed into existing management duties.
- No additional headcount needed.
System Touchpoints: - Budget entry by department, cost center, GL account with monthly phasing (W26.2–5)
- Consolidation of department budgets into entity and group budgets (W26.6)
- Budget loading and lock-down after Board approval (W26.9)
- Budget vs. actual reporting with variance % and drill-down (W26.10–11)
- Budget revision workflow with approval (W26.13)
- Budget availability check during PO and capex creation (links to W2, W21)
Time Estimate: - Annual budget cycle (Q4): ~8–10 weeks total
- CFO budget circular preparation: ~1 week
- Department budget preparation: ~2–3 weeks (Dept. Heads)
- Merchandise purchase budget: ~1–2 weeks (Category Managers)
- Store-level P&L budgets: ~1–2 weeks (VP Store Operations)
- Payroll budget: ~1 week (HR)
- Consolidation and review: ~1 week (Controller)
- CEO/Board negotiation and approval: ~1–2 weeks
- System loading: ~2–3 days (Controller)
- Monthly variance review: ~1 day total effort (~2 hours Controller + ~1 hour each Dept. Head × 10–15 departments + ~1 hour CFO)
- Quarterly budget revision: ~4 hours (Controller) + ~2 hours (CFO review)

fields.Frequency: Daily flash, weekly review, monthly close reporting, quarterly board pack
fields.Participants: Controller, CFO, CEO, Department Heads, BI Analyst
fields.Trigger: Reporting calendar (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly cadences)
fields.Volume: ~50 standard reports on recurring schedules; ~20 ad-hoc requests/month

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "reviews daily flash on mobile dashboard" (replaces manual Step 2).
Controls: - CTL-292 (ensure controlled execution — FP&A & Reporting (PA-17.4).)
- operational: resources and missed early warning signals
Pain Points / Risks: - **Report overload and consumption fatigue**: with ~50 standard reports on recurring schedules plus ~20 ad-hoc requests/month, executives and Department Heads may experience report fatigue; auto-distributed reports that are not reviewed represent wasted system resources and missed early warning signals

- **Store P&L allocation methodology disputes**: DC warehousing costs allocated to stores (proportional to replenishment order value or volume) may disadvantage stores with higher-value/lower-volume merchandise vs. stores with lower-value/higher-volume merchandise; Store Managers may challenge the allocation methodology during monthly reviews

- **Data freshness vs. accuracy tradeoff**: daily flash reports (step 1) rely on near-real-time POS data that may not be fully reconciled; if executives act on unreconciled data (e.g., chasing a negative margin that turns out to be a posting error), credibility of the reporting rhythm is undermined

- **Board pack preparation time compression**: quarterly board packs require consolidating financials, KPI scorecards, risk register updates, and management discussion; with only 5 working days between month-end close and board meetings, the Controller and CFO are under severe time pressure
Staffing Implication: - **1 BI Analyst** (within IT or Finance): Handles ~20 ad-hoc requests/month + maintains standard report templates + supports self-service tool adoption. This may be a new role or absorbed by a data-savvy Finance team member.
- **Controller**: Monthly reporting adds ~8 hours/month (review + variance analysis + board pack quarterly). Absorbed into existing duties.
- Most standard reports are auto-generated; the human effort is in review, interpretation, and action.
System Touchpoints: - Scheduled report auto-generation and distribution (email, portal, mobile) (W35.1, 4, 8–13)
- Executive dashboard with real-time KPIs (W35.2)
- Store P&L module (W35.10)
- Self-service report builder / ad-hoc query tool (W35.18)
- Mobile dashboard for executives (W35.2)
- Integration with all ERP modules (financials, inventory, POS, procurement, HR, ecommerce) for data aggregation

- Store P&L occupancy cost allocation: store rent is a direct charge per location based on individual lease agreements with Property Mgmt Inc. (not allocated from a pool); DC warehousing and distribution costs (IC payment to Logistics Inc. per W14) are allocated to stores monthly based on a configurable allocation key (recommended: proportional to replenishment order value or volume per store); utility costs are direct charges per store (each location has its own meter/account); corporate overhead from Holdings Inc. (management fees per W14) is shown as a separate line below store EBITDA, not embedded in store-level P&L; system auto-generates store P&L with all cost lines from configurable allocation rules

- Store-level budget variance tracking: annual budget (W26) is phased monthly per store with revenue, COGS, labor, occupancy, and shrinkage targets; system generates monthly store budget vs. actual report with variance flags (revenue > ±5%, gross margin > ±2%, operating expense > +10%); Regional Manager reviews store-level budget variance with Store Manager during monthly store visit; significant variances escalated to VP Store Operations; store-level budget accountability is a standing agenda item in monthly management committee meeting (W35.14)
Time Estimate: - Daily flash report: automated (system-generated by 7:00 AM)
- CFO daily flash review: ~5 min/day
- Weekly reports (sales, AP aging, cash flow): automated generation + ~30 min Controller review
- Monthly reporting (financials, variance, store P&L, AR aging, HR metrics): ~8 hours/month (Controller + Chief Accountant)
- Management committee meeting preparation and attendance: ~2–3 hours/month (CFO + Dept. Heads)
- Quarterly board pack preparation: ~8–12 hours/quarter (Controller + CFO)
- Ad-hoc report requests: ~20/month × ~1 hour avg = ~20 hours/month (BI Analyst)
- Total management reporting effort: ~40–50 hours/month across all participants

fields.Frequency: ~50–100 asset disposals/year; peaks during store renovations and IT refresh cycles
fields.Participants: Cost Accountant, Requestor (dept), CFO, IT (for IT assets), Procurement (if resale), Legal (if land/building)
fields.Trigger: Asset reaches end of useful life, becomes uneconomic to maintain, or is replaced by new asset
fields.Volume: ~5,000–8,000 fixed assets across all entities (POS terminals, forklifts, vehicles, fixtures, IT servers, office equipment; per W661)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-request of "Requestor identifies asset for disposal" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-record of "Cost Accountant reviews asset record" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-route of "routed for approval per tier" (replaces manual Step 4).
Controls: - CTL-26 (control fixed asset disposals.)
- operational: Cost Accountant review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Disposal gain/loss volatility hitting P&L**: disposing of assets with significant net book value (e.g., store fixtures during early lease termination per W45) can generate material disposal losses that distort period-over-period P&L comparisons; CFO must explain these one-time impacts during management committee meetings (W35)

- **IT asset data wiping compliance risk**: failure to properly wipe data from POS terminals, laptops, and servers before disposal violates RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act) and exposes the company to NPC fines and reputational damage; tracking data wipe certification across 200 stores with distributed IT equipment is operationally challenging; mitigated by CTL-26 (control fixed asset disposals)

- **Stolen or missing assets discovered during disposal review**: when Cost Accountant reviews asset records for disposal, the asset may already be physically missing (theft, undocumented transfer, or unrecorded disposal); this triggers investigation workflows involving Internal Audit, Store Manager, and potentially Legal

- **Resale value realization for used retail fixtures**: the secondary market for used store fixtures (shelving, racking, lighting) in the Philippines is limited; expected resale proceeds often fall short of initial valuation estimates, resulting in larger disposal losses than budgeted
Staffing Implication: - **Cost Accountant**: 50–100 disposals/year × ~30 min each = ~25–50 hours/year = ~2–4 hours/month. Absorbed within existing Finance team.
- No incremental headcount needed.
System Touchpoints: - Fixed asset disposal workflow with approval tiers (W39.4)
- Asset record with NBV calculation at any point (W39.2)
- Disposal entry auto-generation: cost removal, depreciation reversal, gain/loss calculation (W39.9)
- Asset status lifecycle: Active → Pending Disposal → Disposed (W39.10)
- Disposal gain/loss reporting (W39.11)
- Integration with W21 (Capex → Asset creation) for full asset lifecycle tracking
Time Estimate: - Disposal request initiation: ~15 min/asset (requestor)
- Asset record review and NBV calculation: ~15 min/asset (Cost Accountant)
- Disposal valuation (material assets): ~1–2 hours/asset (requestor)
- Approval per tier: ~15–30 min/asset
- Disposal method determination and execution: ~15–30 min/asset (varies by method)
- IT data wipe (if applicable): ~30 min/asset (IT Team)
- Disposal entry posting: ~15 min/asset (Cost Accountant)
- Quarterly disposal review: ~30 min/quarter (Cost Accountant)
- Total: ~50–100 disposals/year × ~1–2 hours avg = ~50–200 hours/year (~4–17 hours/month)

steps.activity: Requestor identifies asset for disposal: reason (end of life, beyond repair, obsolete, replacement, store closure)
Cost Accountant reviews asset record: original cost, accumulated depreciation, net book value (NBV), remaining useful life, any outstanding encumbrances
If NBV is material (> PHP 50,000): Requestor obtains disposal valuation or market quotation for resale
Disposal request routed for approval per tier: (a) NBV ≤ PHP 50,000: Controller, (b) NBV PHP 50,001–500,000: CFO, (c) NBV > PHP 500,000: CEO, (d) Land/building: Board
Cost Accountant determines disposal method: (a) trade-in (against new asset purchase), (b) public sale/auction, (c) scrap/recycle, (d) donation, (e) write-off (no residual value)
If sale: Procurement or Admin conducts sale; system records proceeds
If IT asset: IT ensures data wipe and compliance with Data Privacy Act (RA 10173) before physical disposal
Physical disposal or handover executed; asset tag removed; documented with photos

Cost Accountant posts disposal entry in system: (a) remove asset at original cost from fixed asset register, (b) remove accumulated depreciation, (c) recognize gain/loss on disposal = proceeds − NBV (or NBV if scrapped), (d) post to GL disposal P&L account
System updates fixed asset register; asset status changed to "Disposed" with disposal date; asset no longer depreciated
Quarterly: Cost Accountant reviews disposed assets report; reconciles disposal gain/loss to GL

fields.Frequency: Monthly margin monitoring; quarterly deep-dive review; annual category-level strategy review
fields.Participants: Cost Accountant, Controller, Category Managers, Pricing Analysts, VP Merchandising, CFO

Background: Product costing and margin analysis is currently fragmented: WAC verification happens during month-end close (W9A.6a), margin impact assessment occurs during price changes (W40.2), and assortment review (W1) considers category-level margin targets. This workflow consolidates these into a structured periodic review that ensures margin erosion is detected early, cost changes are proactively managed, and pricing strategy decisions are data-driven. It bridges the Finance and Merchandising functions.
Controls: - CTL-292 (ensure controlled execution — FP&A & Reporting (PA-17.4).)
- operational: may not handle automatically
Pain Points / Risks: - **WAC distortion from small-quantity high-cost receipts**: a single small receipt at an unusually high unit cost (e.g., air-freighted emergency replenishment) can shift the WAC for that SKU upward, making margin analysis misleading for the entire month until the weighted average normalizes

- **Promotional margin leakage going undetected**: promotional pricing (W13) is approved based on planned margin, but actual sell-through mix and cannibalization effects may result in realized margins significantly below plan; the monthly margin report may flag the issue too late for corrective action within the promo period

- **Cross-functional margin accountability disputes**: margin erosion is blamed on cost increases (Merchandising/Vendor), pricing pressure (Pricing/Sales), or promotional discounting (Marketing); without clear root cause attribution in the margin exception report, cross-functional meetings devolve into blame-shifting rather than action

- **Import vs. domestic cost comparability challenges**: landed cost for imported goods includes duty, freight, insurance, and FX conversion — all variable month to month; comparing import vs. domestic margin requires normalizing for these factors, which the system may not handle automatically
Staffing Implication: - **Cost Accountant**: adds ~4 hours/month for monthly review + ~12 hours/quarter for deep-dive + ~16 hours/year for annual review = ~100 hours/year. Absorbed within existing Finance team.
- **Pricing Analysts**: add ~4 hours/quarter for joint pricing strategy recommendations. Absorbed.
- **No incremental headcount.**
System Touchpoints: - Automated monthly margin analysis report: category-level and SKU-level margin % with trend comparison (W85.1)
- Margin exception reporting: SKUs below threshold with root cause classification (W85.3)
- Quarterly category margin deep-dive: vendor-level analysis, import vs. domestic, promo vs. non-promo (W85.5)
- Configurable margin thresholds per category with alerting (W85.8)
- Annual margin strategy report with driver analysis and proposed targets (W85.9)

- Integration with W1 (assortment review — margin is a key input to SKU add/drop decisions), W9A (WAC verification and month-end inventory valuation), W13 (promo margin impact), W27 (vendor rebate impact on effective margin), W40 (SRP changes — margin impact calculator), W44 (vendor cost negotiation), W61 (competitive pricing pressure), W68 (product discontinuation — margin as exit criterion), W83 (campaign ROI — margin data feeds campaign performance analysis)
Time Estimate: - Monthly margin report generation: automated

Background: Bank reconciliation is a fundamental financial control ensuring that the general ledger cash balances match actual bank balances. With 5 legal entities, ~25 bank accounts across 4 banks (BDO, BPI, Metrobank, Chinabank), multi-currency (PHP and USD), and high transaction volume from store deposits, vendor payments, payroll crediting, and ecommerce settlement, a structured reconciliation workflow is essential. This workflow is distinct from W30 (daily treasury cash position management) which focuses on operational cash visibility; bank reconciliation is the periodic accounting control that validates GL accuracy.
Controls: - CTL-19 (ensure bank reconciliation completeness.); CTL-47 (ensure ecommerce payment reconciliation accuracy.)
- operational: Treasury Analyst review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Multi-Entity Considerations: - Each entity's bank accounts reconciled separately
- Intercompany bank transfers (W14 settlements) must clear in both entities' bank reconciliations in the same month
- USD accounts (for import payments) reconciled with FX revaluation per W9A.5a
- Ecommerce payment gateway accounts (PayMongo, Dragonpay) reconciled via W99 and cross-referenced here
Pain Points / Risks: - **High-volume unmatched items from 200 store deposits**: with 200 stores making daily cash deposits, the volume of unmatched bank statement lines is substantial; store deposit discrepancies (shortages, delayed deposits, wrong amount) each require investigation with the individual Store Manager, creating a bottleneck during month-end

- **Multi-bank format inconsistency**: BDO, BPI, Metrobank, and Chinabank each change their electronic statement formats periodically; when a format changes, the auto-matching engine fails and Treasury Analysts must manually process that bank's accounts until the ERP format mapping is updated

- **Stale check accumulation**: checks issued but not presented within 6 months per Philippine law must be reversed; tracking outstanding checks across 5 entities and ~25 bank accounts is manual and error-prone, with stale check reversals often discovered only during external audit (W95)

- **USD account FX revaluation complexity**: USD bank accounts require monthly FX revaluation at BIR-prescribed exchange rates; any discrepancy between the revalued GL balance and the actual bank statement USD balance (converted at month-end rate) creates reconciling items that are difficult to explain to non-Finance stakeholders
Staffing Implication: - **Treasury Analysts**: ~25 accounts × ~90 min each = ~37.5 hours/month. With 2 Treasury Analysts, that's ~19 hours each/month. Absorbed within existing Finance team (month-end close week is the heaviest period).
- **Controller**: 1 hour/month for review. Absorbed.
- **No incremental headcount.**
System Touchpoints: - Electronic bank statement import (BDO, BPI, Metrobank, Chinabank file formats) (W89.1)
- Auto-matching engine: payment reference, deposit reference, batch reference matching with confidence scoring (W89.2)
- Bank reconciliation module with GL-to-bank matching screen (W89.3–4)
- Outstanding items aging tracker with escalation triggers (W89.5, W89.9)
- Auto-journal entry generation for bank charges, interest, FX, stale checks (W89.8)

- Integration with W7 (AP payments), W8 (AR receipts), W10 (payroll bank files), W14 (IC settlements), W21 (capex payments), W25 (petty cash replenishment), W30 (treasury sweeps), W90 (tax payments), W99 (payment gateway settlements)
Time Estimate: - Bank statement import (all accounts): ~30 min/account × ~25 accounts = ~12.5 hours
- Auto-match review: ~15 min/account × ~25 accounts = ~6.25 hours
- Manual matching and unmatched investigation: ~30 min/account × ~25 accounts = ~12.5 hours
- Outstanding items review: ~15 min/account × ~25 accounts = ~6.25 hours
- Reconciliation sign-off: ~5 min/account × ~25 accounts = ~2 hours
- Controller review: ~1 hour/month
- Journal entry posting: automated
- Total bank reconciliation: ~37.5 hours/month (spread across 2 Treasury Analysts, concentrated during close week days 3–5)

steps.activity: **Statement import**: Treasury Analyst imports electronic bank statements (BDO, BPI, Metrobank, Chinabank formats) into ERP bank reconciliation module; for accounts receiving paper statements only, AP Clerk scans and enters key transactions manually

**Auto-matching — system level**: System attempts to auto-match bank statement lines to GL transactions: (a) vendor payment (W7) matched by payment reference and amount, (b) customer receipt (W8) matched by deposit reference, (c) payroll bank file (W10) matched by batch reference and total, (d) intercompany settlement (W14) matched by IC reference, (e) treasury sweeps and transfers (W30) matched by transfer reference, (f) tax payments (W90) matched by BIR payment reference, (g) capex payments (W21) matched by PO/invoice reference

**Review auto-matched items**: Treasury Analyst reviews auto-matched items for accuracy; system displays match confidence score (high: exact reference + amount match; medium: amount match only; low: fuzzy match); high-confidence matches auto-accepted; medium and low reviewed manually

**Manual matching — unmatched items**: Treasury Analyst investigates unmatched bank statement lines: (a) bank charges and fees (not in GL — post as bank charges expense), (b) deposit discrepancies (store cash deposit variance per W5F), (c) timing differences (checks issued but not yet cleared), (d) unknown items requiring investigation, (e) payment gateway settlement deposits (cross-reference W99), (f) interest income/expense (post as incurred)

**Outstanding items review**: (a) Outstanding checks > 90 days: investigate with AP — stale check per Philippine law (6 months); if stale, AP re-issues or reverses; (b) Outstanding deposits > 7 days: investigate with store operations — missing deposit; (c) Unrecorded bank fees: post to bank charges expense; (d) FX gains/losses on USD accounts: post FX revaluation per W9A.5a

**Reconciliation sign-off**: Treasury Analyst completes bank reconciliation per account; system generates reconciliation report showing: opening GL balance, plus/minus reconciling items, ending GL balance, ending bank balance, unreconciled difference (must be zero); Treasury Analyst signs off electronically

**Controller review**: Controller reviews completed bank reconciliations for all accounts; focuses on: (a) accounts with high unmatched volume, (b) unusual items, (c) stale checks, (d) deposit discrepancies > PHP 5,000; approves or returns for correction

**Journal entries**: System auto-generates journal entries for: (a) bank charges and fees, (b) interest income, (c) FX gains/losses on USD accounts, (d) stale check reversals, (e) deposit discrepancy adjustments; all auto-posted to GL with bank reconciliation reference

**Aging of reconciling items**: System tracks aging of all unreconciled items: items > 30 days flagged for Treasury Analyst follow-up; items > 60 days escalated to Controller; items > 90 days require write-off or resolution per Controller

Background: With 200 stores generating ~PHP 5.04B in monthly in-store revenue across diverse geographies (urban Metro Manila vs. provincial Mindanao), store-level profitability varies significantly. Store Managers need actionable financial visibility to manage their P&L, Regional Managers need comparative store performance, and CFO needs consolidated chain performance. A manually generated store P&L process would require 200 custom reports monthly — impractical without automation. The ERP must auto-generate store P&Ls with standardized cost allocation, enabling consistent comparison across the chain.
Controls: - CTL-292 (ensure controlled execution — FP&A & Reporting (PA-17.4).)
- operational: FP&A Manager review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Overhead allocation disputes**: Store Managers may dispute their allocated overhead share (corporate IT, HR, Marketing costs distributed by revenue or sqm); a small store with PHP 15M/month revenue absorbs the same overhead rate as a PHP 35M/month store, making small stores appear less profitable

- **Rent expense distortion**: stores leasing from BuildRight Property Management Inc. at varying rates (older leases vs. newer leases in premium locations) create P&L comparison distortion that is unrelated to store operating performance

- **COGS timing mismatches**: if inventory adjustments, purchase price variances, or inter-DC transfers (W22) are posted after the store P&L is generated, the COGS and margin figures will be inaccurate; FP&A Analyst must verify all inventory transactions are finalized before P&L generation

- **Store Manager financial literacy**: many Store Managers are operations-focused and may struggle to interpret P&L line items, variances, and contribution margin concepts; Regional Manager coaching is essential for P&L to drive action
Staffing Implication: - FP&A Analyst: ~6 hours/month on store P&L review and publication; absorbed within existing FP&A team
- FP&A Manager: ~2 hours/month on review + 8 hours/quarter on trend analysis; absorbed
- Store Managers: ~1–2 hours/month each; absorbed (part of monthly management routine per W67)
- Regional Managers: ~4–6 hours/month each; absorbed
- No incremental headcount
System Touchpoints: - Automated store P&L generation engine: revenue (POS, ecommerce, trade), COGS (WAC-based), direct expenses (payroll, rent, utilities, maintenance), contribution margin, allocated overhead, net income (W1405.1)
- Variance analysis engine: current vs. prior month, current vs. same month PY, YTD vs. budget; materiality thresholds configurable per line item (W1405.2)
- Regional P&L roll-up with inter-store comparison metrics: revenue/sqm, gross margin %, labor cost %, contribution margin/employee (W1405.4)
- Store P&L portal: Store Manager and Regional Manager access individual store and regional P&L with drill-down to department and expense category (W1405.5)

- Integration with W9A (month-end close — trigger), W5B (POS — revenue data), W10 (payroll — labor cost allocation), W14 (IC rent — rent expense), W47 (facility maintenance — maintenance expense), W26 (budget — variance comparison), W231 (QBR — quarterly trend analysis), W67 (store performance review — operational KPI feed)
Time Estimate: - System auto-generation: ~17 hours (batch) — automated, no human time
- FP&A anomaly review: ~4 hours/month
- P&L publication and distribution: ~2 hours/month

steps.activity: System auto-generates store-level P&L after month-end close is finalized (W9A completion trigger): (a) **Revenue**: POS sales by department (Lumber, Plumbing/Electrical, Tiles, Tools/Hardware, Paint, Appliances, Garden, Other) + ecommerce revenue allocated to ship-from-store location + trade account revenue + installation service revenue; (b) **Cost of Goods Sold**: WAC-based inventory cost per item sold, allocated by store; includes landed cost components (freight, duty, insurance) per SKU; (c) **Gross Margin**: revenue minus COGS by department and overall; (d) **Direct Store Operating Expenses**: store labor cost (from payroll W10 allocation), rent (to Property Mgmt Inc. per W14), utilities (electricity, water, internet), store-level maintenance and supplies (W47), store-level LP costs, depreciation of store fixtures and equipment; (e) **Contribution Margin**: gross margin minus direct store operating expenses; (f) **Allocated Overhead**: regional management cost, corporate overhead allocation (IT, HR, Finance, Marketing) allocated by revenue or selling area; (g) **Store Net Income**: contribution margin minus allocated overhead

steps.activity: System generates variance analysis: current month vs. prior month, current month vs. same month prior year, current month vs. budget (W26), and year-to-date vs. budget; variances flagged as favorable (green) or unfavorable (red) with percentage deviation; material variances (> 5% of line item or > PHP 100,000) highlighted for investigation

Background: Between monthly store P&Ls (W1405), BuildRight leadership needs weekly visibility into sales performance to detect trends, identify underperforming stores early, and respond to competitive or seasonal shifts in real time. The weekly flash report is a streamlined, action-oriented document focused on revenue, transaction counts, and key retail KPIs — not a full P&L. It serves as the primary early warning system for the executive team, enabling course correction before month-end.
Controls: - CTL-292 (ensure controlled execution — FP&A & Reporting (PA-17.4).)
- operational: FP&A Analyst review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Typhoon week distortion**: a week with typhoon-related store closures in one region will show a dramatic chain-wide revenue decline that is not representative of underlying performance; narrative commentary must contextualize these events to prevent overreaction

- **POS data latency**: stores operating in offline mode (W5G) may not have all transactions uploaded by the Monday 6:00 AM extraction; flash report may understate the prior week's revenue by 1–2%; automatically reconciled in following week's report

- **Executive attention fatigue**: weekly reports can become routine and ignored if consistently showing "within normal range"; exception-based alerting (automatic email only when variances exceed threshold) mitigates, while full dashboard remains available on-demand

- **Category attribution accuracy**: promotional revenue attribution depends on correct promo SKU tagging at POS (W523); if promotional quick-keys are not set up correctly, promotional revenue is understated and regular revenue is overstated
Staffing Implication: - FP&A Analyst: ~2 hours/week on flash report; primary weekly deliverable; absorbed within existing FP&A team
- FP&A Manager: ~30 min/week on review; absorbed
- Executives: ~15 min/week on stand-up; absorbed within executive calendar
- No incremental headcount
System Touchpoints: - Automated weekly data extraction from POS, ecommerce, and trade account transaction tables (W1406.1)
- KPI calculation engine: WoW, WPLY, WTD vs. budget, MTD vs. budget, YTD vs. budget, ATV, UPT, sales/sqm, sales/employee (W1406.2)
- Visual dashboard: 13-week trend, regional waterfall, store heat map, top/bottom 10, category breakdown, ecommerce metrics, executive scorecard (W1406.3)
- Automated distribution: executive summary email, portal link, regional manager summaries (W1406.5)
- Mid-week update trigger: automated alert when chain-wide or regional variance exceeds threshold (W1406.7)

- Integration with W5B (POS — transaction data), W11/W19 (ecommerce — online revenue), W5F (store closing — daily revenue reconciliation), W83 (campaign — promotional revenue attribution), W1405 (store P&L — monthly context for weekly trends), W67 (store performance — operational KPI alignment)
Time Estimate: - System auto-generation: ~30 min (batch processing + dashboard rendering)

steps.activity: System auto-extracts prior week's (Monday–Sunday) transaction data from POS, ecommerce, and trade account systems: total revenue by store, by region, and by channel; transaction count; average transaction value (ATV); units per transaction (UPT); sales per sqm; sales per employee

System calculates key metrics and comparisons: (a) week-over-week revenue change (% and PHP), (b) same-week-prior-year revenue change (% and PHP), (c) week-to-date (WTD) revenue vs. weekly budget target, (d) month-to-date (MTD) revenue vs. monthly budget target, (e) year-to-date (YTD) revenue vs. annual budget target, (f) top 10 and bottom 10 stores by revenue growth vs. prior year, (g) ecommerce revenue as % of total, (h) BOPIS vs. delivery order split, (i) trade/B2B revenue as % of total, (j) promotional revenue as % of total (from active promotions per W83)

System generates visual dashboard with: (a) chain-wide revenue trend (13-week rolling chart), (b) regional revenue waterfall (5 store regions per profile §3.1: Mindanao, Visayas, Luzon-outside-NCR, Metro Manila, North/Central Luzon), (c) store heat map (green/yellow/red by performance vs. budget), (d) top 10 / bottom 10 store list, (e) category revenue breakdown (Lumber, Tiles, Plumbing, etc.), (f) ecommerce channel metrics, (g) executive KPI scorecard

FP&A Analyst reviews auto-generated flash report for data quality: verifies POS revenue totals reconcile to daily cash/card/e-wallet settlements (W5F, W537, W1268), flags stores with missing or anomalous data (e.g., store showing zero revenue for a day — possible POS system issue), and adds narrative commentary on notable items (weather events, typhoons, holidays, competitor openings)
